item.title: The Basket of Apples
item.lesson: Look carefully at the table: its left edge and right edge do not line up. The bottle leans; the cookies at right are seen from the side and from above at once; the basket tilts forward farther than physics allows without spilling. None of this is error. Cézanne, working in near-isolation in Provence, had concluded that honest painting must record how we actually see — from two eyes, over time, in glances that never fuse into a single frozen viewpoint. So he built his still lifes from multiple perspectives simultaneously and welded them together with color instead of line. 'With an apple,' he said, 'I will astonish Paris.' It took decades, but when Paris finally looked, everything cracked open: Picasso and Braque took the multiplied viewpoints straight into Cubism, and Matisse and Picasso both called him 'the father of us all.' Every apple here weighs more than fruit should — because each one is a small argument about the nature of seeing.
item.lookFor: Follow the table's front edge from left to right: it visibly breaks and re-joins at a different height behind the white cloth. Cézanne left the seam in plain sight, daring you to notice how your eye forgives it.
